newsitem.title: UK: Greenpeace protestors occupy BP Aberdeen roof.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace protestors occupy BP Aberdeen roof.

text.p: Environmental lobby group Greenpeace on Wednesday stepped up its campaign against the oil industry in Britain in a raid on the Scottish offices of British Petroleum.

Greenpeace said it installed 25 solar panels on the roof of BP Exploration headquarters in Aberdeen and called on the company to switch investment from Atlantic frontier oil exploration to solar power.
"BP admits that climate change is a serious problem, well it's time they put their money where their mouth is," said Greenpeace campaigner Marcus Rand.
The green group has targeted BP for its leading role in developing a new site in deep Atlantic waters west of Scotland's Shetland islands.
A team of 20 activists scaled the building to install the panels made by BP's solar subsidiary and put up a sign reading "BP, Solar not Oil."
The protest comes a day before BP holds its Annual General Meeting in London.
A spokesman for BP in Aberdeen said three or four activists were still on the roof, adding that they could stay there as long as they liked providing they caused no damage.

Greenpeace called on BP to invest 100 million pounds ($162.6 million) in solar power which it said would create 40,000 new jobs in Britain. It said the oil company had only spent 60 million in the past 10 years and had failed even to install solar panels on any of its offices in Britain.
"BP produces all its solar panels overseas," said Greenpeace's Rand. "At the moment you could sum up BP's attitude to solar as 'made in Spain, sold in Japan, ignored in Britain'."
"Climate change requires international agreements not piecemeal action," said the BP spokesman.
"The issue here is that we all rely on oil, whether for transport, heating, contact lenses or CDs. We cannot function as a society without oil and gas.
BP is expected in the next few weeks to bring on stream its Foinaven development the first of a new generation of oilfields on the Atlantic frontier.
"We are going about our lawful business and in the process creating thousands of jobs in Scotland right now," said the BP spokesman of the development.
Last month Greenpeace raised a challenge to Britain's oil industry by bidding for rights to 22,000 square miles of offshore acreage available in Britain's 17th oil licensing round.
It said it hoped to block the multi-billion dollar aspirations of the oil industry and turn the site into a marine wildlife sanctuary.
The British government rejected the bid.
In 1995, Greenpeace forced Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell to rethink its plans to ditch the Brent Spar platform at sea.
A high profile campaign involved Greenpeace attempts to block the platform being towed to its dumping site and a boycott of Shell petrol stations in Europe.

($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
